slots.practicalActivity: Take a real small dataset you can access (a public dataset like Iris, Titanic, or a retail sample) and classify every column by its measurement scale (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio), writing one sentence per column justifying the classification, then write 2 real questions this course's statistics could answer about that same data.
slots.deliverable: A written table classifying every column of a real dataset by measurement scale, plus 2 specific questions statistics will help answer about it.

slots.practicalActivity: Using Python (pandas/NumPy) or a calculator, compute the mean, median, and mode of a real numeric column (e.g. order totals from a public e-commerce dataset), hand-check at least one value, then add one extreme outlier and recompute all three, writing which measure moved the most and why.
slots.deliverable: Mean/median/mode computed before and after adding one outlier to a real numeric column, with a written explanation of which measure resisted the outlier best.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the range, variance, standard deviation, and IQR of the same numeric column in Python, then identify any values that fall outside 1.5*IQR from the quartiles and flag them.
slots.deliverable: Range/variance/std/IQR calculated in Python for a real numeric column, plus a list of any IQR-flagged outlier values.

slots.practicalActivity: Plot a histogram and a boxplot of the same numeric column with matplotlib, write whether the shape is roughly symmetric, right-skewed, or left-skewed, and state whether the mean or the median better represents the 'typical' value given that shape.
slots.deliverable: A histogram and boxplot of a real numeric column, plus a written shape classification and a stated choice of mean vs. median that the shape justifies.

slots.practicalActivity: Using a real categorical dataset (e.g. Titanic survival, or a retail purchase-by-category table), compute at least 3 basic probabilities (P(event)), one conditional probability (P(A|B)), and test whether two events are independent by comparing P(A|B) to P(A).
slots.deliverable: 3 computed probabilities, 1 conditional probability, and a written independence test comparing P(A|B) to P(A) on real categorical data.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a concrete Bayes' theorem calculation in Python with explicit real-world numbers (e.g. a medical or quality-control test's true/false positive rates and a base rate, computing P(actually positive | tested positive)), and compare the posterior to the naive intuition of just reading the test's accuracy.
slots.deliverable: One Bayes' theorem calculation in Python with stated prior, likelihood, and posterior probabilities, plus a written sentence comparing the posterior to the naive (wrong) intuition.

slots.practicalActivity: Define a discrete random variable from a real scenario (e.g. number of items per order, using its observed frequency distribution), compute its expected value and variance by hand and in Python, then simulate 1000 draws to confirm the simulated mean approaches your calculated expected value.
slots.deliverable: A discrete random variable's expected value and variance computed analytically and confirmed by a 1000-draw Python simulation.

slots.practicalActivity: Model a real-feeling scenario as a Binomial distribution (e.g. probability a customer leaves a review, out of 50 orders) and as a Poisson distribution (e.g. number of support tickets per day given a known average rate), computing exact probabilities for each with scipy.stats.
slots.deliverable: One Binomial probability calculation and one Poisson probability calculation in scipy.stats, each tied to a stated real scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Using scipy.stats.norm, compute the probability that a real-feeling normally distributed measurement (e.g. delivery time with a stated mean and standard deviation) falls within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean, and find the value at the 90th percentile with .ppf().
slots.deliverable: Probabilities for the 68/95/99.7 empirical rule computed with scipy.stats.norm for a stated mean/std, plus the 90th-percentile value via .ppf().

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one non-normal continuous distribution relevant to data work (exponential for time-between-events, or uniform for a random assignment), simulate 1000 draws with NumPy, and plot the simulated histogram against the distribution's theoretical PDF using scipy.stats.
slots.deliverable: 1000 simulated draws from a non-normal continuous distribution plotted against its theoretical PDF curve.

slots.practicalActivity: Distributions lab: simulate and compare at least 3 different distributions from this chapter (one discrete, two continuous) side by side in one notebook, checking each simulation's sample mean/variance against the distribution's theoretical values.
slots.deliverable: One notebook simulating 3 distributions from this chapter with sample statistics compared against theoretical values for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Simulate drawing 1000 random samples (size 30 each) from a known non-normal population (a skewed distribution built with NumPy) and plot the distribution of the 1000 sample means to directly observe the Central Limit Theorem producing a bell shape even though the population wasn't normal; separately, write one example of real sampling bias (e.g. only surveying customers who already left a review) and why it would distort the estimate.
slots.deliverable: A histogram of 1000 sample means from a skewed population demonstrating the CLT, plus a written sampling-bias example and why it distorts results.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the standard error of the mean for a real numeric sample, then build a 95% confidence interval around the sample mean by hand with the SE-based formula and confirm it with scipy.stats, writing a correct one-sentence interpretation of what the interval does and does not claim.
slots.deliverable: A manually-computed standard error and 95% confidence interval, confirmed with scipy.stats, plus a one-sentence correct interpretation of the interval.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a bootstrap confidence interval for the median of a real skewed numeric sample (resampling with replacement 1000+ times in NumPy) and compare it to the formula-based confidence interval from the previous slot, noting where bootstrapping is more appropriate.
slots.deliverable: A 1000+ resample bootstrap confidence interval for a sample median, with a written comparison against a formula-based CI and when bootstrapping is the better choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Sampling & Estimation lab: take a fresh real sample (different data than used above) and report its standard error, a 95% confidence interval via the formula, and a bootstrap confidence interval, writing a short paragraph recommending which number to report to a stakeholder and why.
slots.deliverable: One real dataset's SE, formula-based 95% CI, and bootstrap CI computed side by side, with a written stakeholder recommendation.

slots.practicalActivity: State a real null and alternative hypothesis (e.g. 'the new checkout page does not change average order value'), run a hypothesis test in scipy.stats on simulated or real before/after data, and write exactly what the resulting p-value does and does not mean in plain language.
slots.deliverable: A stated null/alternative hypothesis pair, a computed p-value from a real test, and a plain-language (non-circular) written interpretation of that p-value.

lessons.title: Type I & Type II Errors and Power

slots.practicalActivity: For the test from the previous slot, write out what a Type I error and a Type II error would concretely mean for the business, then compute the statistical power of that test given a stated effect size, sample size, and alpha.
slots.deliverable: A written Type I/Type II error description specific to the business scenario, plus a computed statistical power value for the test's actual sample size.

slots.practicalActivity: Run all 3 t-test variants in scipy.stats on real or realistic simulated data: a one-sample t-test against a target value, a two-sample Welch's t-test comparing two independent groups, and a paired t-test on matched before/after data, reporting the p-value and a Cohen's d effect size for each.
slots.deliverable: 3 completed t-tests (one-sample, two-sample, paired) with scipy.stats output and a Cohen's d effect size for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a chi-square test of independence on a real 2-way categorical table (e.g. purchase category by region) and a one-way ANOVA comparing a numeric outcome (e.g. order value) across 3+ groups (e.g. 3 marketing channels), interpreting both p-values.
slots.deliverable: One chi-square test result on a real categorical table and one ANOVA result across 3+ real groups, each with a written interpretation.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a post-hoc Tukey HSD test (statsmodels) following up on the ANOVA from the previous slot to find which specific group pairs differ, and separately demonstrate the multiple-comparisons problem by running 20 independent t-tests on random noise data and counting how many come back 'significant' at alpha=0.05 by chance alone.
slots.deliverable: A Tukey HSD post-hoc result naming which group pairs significantly differ, plus a simulation showing the false-positive count from 20 tests on pure noise.

slots.practicalActivity: Hypothesis Testing lab: given one real dataset, choose and justify the correct test (t-test, chi-square, or ANOVA) for 3 different real questions about it, run each test, apply a multiple-comparisons correction where more than one test is run, and write a one-paragraph summary of findings.
slots.deliverable: 3 correctly-chosen and executed hypothesis tests on one real dataset, with a multiple-comparisons correction applied and a written summary of findings.

slots.practicalActivity: Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between two real numeric variables that are plausibly correlated but not causally linked, then write a specific plausible confounding variable that could explain the correlation without either variable causing the other.
slots.deliverable: A computed correlation coefficient between two real variables, plus a written, specific confounder hypothesis explaining the correlation without causation.

slots.practicalActivity: Fit a simple linear regression (scipy.stats.linregress or statsmodels) predicting a real numeric outcome from one real predictor, report the slope, intercept, and R-squared, and write what the slope concretely means in the original units.
slots.deliverable: A fitted simple linear regression with slope, intercept, and R-squared reported, plus a plain-language sentence explaining the slope in real units.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a real A/B test (pick one primary metric, randomization unit, alpha, power, and minimum detectable effect, and calculate the required sample size per group with the two-proportion formula), then simulate the resulting data for both groups and analyze it with a two-proportion z-test or t-test, stating whether the design's planned effect was detected.
slots.deliverable: A written A/B test design (metric, sample size calculation) plus a completed analysis of simulated results from that exact design, stating whether the planned effect was detected.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the A/B test analysis from the previous slot and demonstrate 2 real statistical pitfalls on it: show via a small simulation how p-hacking by peeking at the data every day inflates the false-positive rate, and show how stopping the test early on a lucky result would have given a different, wrong conclusion.
slots.deliverable: A simulation demonstrating inflated false positives from early peeking, plus a written comparison of the early-stop conclusion versus the full-sample conclusion from the same simulated A/B test.

slots.practicalActivity: Correlation, Causation & Experiments practice: pick a real public dataset with at least 2 groups and run a complete correlation-to-causation review: compute a correlation, propose and test a confounder if possible, fit a regression, and write a one-page 'what would need to be true for this to be causal' argument.
slots.deliverable: One real-dataset analysis combining correlation, regression, and a written causal-inference argument addressing at least one confounder.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: An End-to-End Statistical Analysis

slots.practicalActivity: Choose one real, publicly available dataset (not used elsewhere in the course) and write a complete analysis plan: 2-3 statistical questions, which specific technique from the course answers each (confidence interval, hypothesis test, regression, etc.), and what a stakeholder would do differently depending on the result.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone plan naming the chosen dataset, 2-3 statistical questions, the specific technique for each, and the decision each result would drive.

slots.practicalActivity: Execute the full capstone plan: compute descriptive statistics, build at least one confidence interval, run at least one hypothesis test, and fit a regression or correlation analysis as planned, on the real chosen dataset.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone notebook/script with descriptive stats, a confidence interval, a hypothesis test, and a regression/correlation analysis, all run on the real chosen dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-to-two-page portfolio writeup of the capstone findings in plain language for a non-technical stakeholder, including the main numeric results, honest caveats about sample size or assumptions, and a clear recommendation.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page plain-language portfolio writeup of the capstone analysis with numeric results, caveats, and a stated recommendation.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can describe a dataset statistically, build confidence intervals, choose and run the right hypothesis test (t-test, chi-square, ANOVA), design and analyze an A/B test, and tell correlation apart from causation -- the statistical reasoning every model and business decision in the rest of the Data Scientist path depends on.
